newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan urges loyalty after South Africa pullout.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan urges loyalty after South Africa pullout.

text.p: Taiwan scrambled on Thursday to limit the damage of South Africa's decision to sever ties in favour of Beijing, urging its 29 other allies not to be swayed by China.
South African President Nelson Mandela said on Wednesday that Pretoria would switch diplomatic ties to Beijing from Taipei by the end of 1997, leaving isolated Taiwan in shock.
"We hope such a situation won't affect our diplomatic relations with other countries...," Foreign Minister John Chang said in a televised news conference.
"Our relations (with South Africa) should not be sacrificed just because South Africa wants to have new relations with communist China. It's not reasonable (to do so)," Chang said.
China on Thursday welcomed South Africa's decision.

"We ... welcome President Nelson Mandela's positive statement concerning normalisation of relations between China and South Africa," Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Cui Tiankai told a news briefing.

South Africa is the biggest of just 30 countries -- mostly underdeveloped states in central America and Africa -- that recognise Taiwan's exiled Republic of China government rather than the communist People's Republic on the mainland.
Taiwan and China have been separated since a civil war ended in 1949. Both governments say they want reunification but so far have refused to talk to each other about how to achieve it.
China sees Taiwan as a renegade province not entitled to foreign ties while Taiwan insists its 21 million people have a right not to be excluded from international activities.
"We will actively negotiate with South Africa in the next 12 months," Chang said, adding that he might visit South Africa before a scheduled January official visit.
"Facing the new situation, we have to take effective and active measures to encounter the situation," Chang said.

Although Chang did not ask Taiwanese businesses to take action, local business giant Tuntex Distinct Corp said it would give the government the final say on its scheduled US$3.0 billion petrochemical project in South Africa.
"We will fully back the government's effort to extend our foreign ties," Tuntex said in a statement.
Taiwanese officials blamed China for South Africa's decision to switch ties, saying China was "buying" foreign ties and damaging chances for reunification between the longtime rivals.
"The origin of this issue is communist China," government spokesman Su Chi quoted Premier Lien Chan as saying after a morning cabinet meeting.

"This shows communist China is intensifying its repression of us internationally. Its moves to buy foreign relations will not do any good for cross-strait relations or national reunification," Lien was quoted as saying.

"We can only say that communist China has no intention to develop bilateral relations in a smooth direction," said Chan Chih-hung, a director of the cabinet's Mainland Affairs Council, Taiwan's top China policymaking body.
There were no protests at Pretoria's embassy, contrasting with the public outrage displayed in recent years after Washington, Seoul and other erstwhile allies dropped Taipei for Beijing.
The switch even took Pretoria's Taipei envoy by surprise.
"I am sad at the moment," ambassador Johannes Viljoen told reporters after being summoned by Chang on Thursday. "I was not informed beforehand by my government."
Viljoen urged Taiwan not to exact reprisals against Pretoria while Chang said Taipei would conduct an overall review of billions of dollars of Taiwanese investments in South Africa.
